title: How a car works: from fuel to wheels
summary: See how tiny bursts of burning fuel become the turning wheels of a petrol car.
objective: Trace how a petrol car turns burning fuel into spinning wheels, and pick the right gear for the job.

hook.prompt: Inside a petrol car's engine, how does the fuel burn?

options.text: In one steady flame, like a gas stove
options.feedback: A steady flame would only heat the engine. Something has to push the car along.

options.text: In thousands of quick, separate bursts every minute
It doesn't burn: it boils water into steam
options.feedback: That's how old steam trains worked. A car engine burns the fuel itself, right inside the engine.

hook.explanation: It burns in quick bursts: at highway speed, each cylinder fires roughly 20 times a second. Each burst gives one push. But a push on what?

bricks.title: Each burst pushes a piston
bricks.body: An engine has several **cylinders**: metal tubes, each with a **piston** that slides up and down inside, like a plunger. A **spark plug** lights a little fuel mixed with air above the piston. It burns in a flash, and the hot gas expands fast, shoving the piston down. That push, repeated thousands of times a minute, is what moves the car.

term.definition: A solid plug that slides up and down inside a cylinder and gets pushed by the burning fuel.

visual.alt: A cylinder with a spark plug on top, burning fuel and air in the space below it, and a piston underneath being pushed down.

bricks.prompt: Tap the part that the burning fuel pushes to move the car.
bricks.hint: Which part can slide up and down?
bricks.explanation: The **piston** is the part that moves. The spark plug only lights the mix, and the space above is where it burns.

bricks.prompt: When the fuel and air burn, what actually shoves the piston down?

options.text: The hot gas expanding
The electric spark itself
options.feedback: The spark only lights the mix. It's far too small to push anything; the expanding gas does the shoving.

options.text: Fuel squirting in under pressure
options.feedback: The fuel arrives before anything burns. The push comes after it burns, when the hot gas expands.

bricks.hint: What happens to gas when it suddenly gets very hot?
bricks.explanation: Burning turns the small mix into very hot gas that expands fast. With nowhere else to go, it shoves the piston down.

bricks.title: Four strokes: suck, squeeze, bang, blow
bricks.body:
So far, one burst gives one push. To keep going, each cylinder repeats four **strokes**:
1. **Intake**: the piston moves down, sucking in fuel and air.
2. **Compression**: it moves up, squeezing the mix.
3. **Power**: the spark lights it, and the burst drives the piston down.
4. **Exhaust**: it moves up, pushing burnt gas out the exhaust pipe.
Only power pushes, so the cylinders take turns firing.

term.definition: One move of the piston, either up or down.

visual.html:
1. IntakeSuck ↓
2. CompressionSqueeze ↑
3. PowerBang ↓
4. ExhaustBlow ↑
visual.alt: Four cylinders in a row: intake with the piston down and fuel drawn in, compression with it up, power with burning gas pushing it down, exhaust with it up.

bricks.prompt: A piston has just moved up, squeezing the fuel and air tight. What happens next?

options.text: The spark lights the mix and the burst drives the piston down
The piston moves down and sucks in fresh fuel and air
options.feedback: That's intake, which comes before the squeeze. A squeezed mix is ready to burn, so power comes next.

options.text: The piston pushes the burnt gas out
options.feedback: Nothing has burnt yet. Exhaust comes after the power stroke, once there's burnt gas to clear.

bricks.hint: Has the squeezed mix burnt yet?
bricks.explanation: The squeeze is the compression stroke. Next comes power: the spark lights the tight mix and the burst drives the piston down.

bricks.prompt: In a four-cylinder engine, one spark plug stops sparking. What happens?

options.text: The engine keeps running, but it shakes and feels weaker
The whole engine stops at once
options.feedback: The other three cylinders still get their sparks and keep taking turns to push, so the engine keeps going.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the other plugs cover for it
options.feedback: That cylinder's mix never burns, so it never makes its power stroke. The engine loses a quarter of its pushes.

bricks.hint: How many cylinders are still pushing?
bricks.explanation: Without a spark, that cylinder never makes its power stroke. The other three still push in turn, so the engine runs, but roughly and with less power.

bricks.title: From up-and-down to spinning wheels
bricks.body: So far, pistons only go up and down, but wheels need to spin. Each piston pushes a rod that turns the **crankshaft**, the way your legs turn a bike's pedals. That spin passes through the **gearbox** to the wheels. A **low gear** turns the wheels slowly but strongly: good for starting and hills. A **high gear** turns them fast while the engine turns slowly: good for cruising, but weak.

term.definition: The shaft that turns the pistons' up-and-down pushes into a spin.

visual.html:
Pistons

Pushed up and down by the bursts

↓

Crankshaft

Turns the pushes into a spin

↓

Gearbox

Low gear: slow but strong. High gear: fast but weak.

↓

Wheels

Spin and move the car
visual.alt: A chain from top to bottom: pistons push the crankshaft, which spins the gearbox, which turns the wheels.

bricks.prompt: Pistons only move up and down, yet the wheels spin round. Which part makes that change?

options.text: The crankshaft
The gearbox
options.feedback: The gearbox receives a spin that's already turning and changes how fast and strong it is. The crankshaft makes the spin.

options.text: The spark plug
options.feedback: The spark plug only lights the mix. It doesn't move anything itself.

bricks.hint: Think of legs pushing a bike's pedals.
bricks.explanation: Each piston's rod pushes on the crankshaft like legs on pedals, so the straight up-and-down pushes become a spin.

bricks.prompt: You're pulling away from a stop at the bottom of a steep hill in a manual car. Which gear makes it easiest?

options.text: A low gear
A high gear
options.feedback: High gears turn the wheels fast but weakly. From a standstill on a hill, the car needs slow, strong turning.

options.text: It makes no difference which gear
options.feedback: Gears change how strongly the wheels turn, and a steep start needs the strongest turning.

bricks.hint: Do you need speed here, or strength?
bricks.explanation: A low gear turns the wheels slowly but strongly, which is exactly what a heavy car needs to get moving uphill.

challenge.prompt: A driver crawls up a steep hill at walking pace, still in the highest gear. The engine shudders and nearly stalls. Why?

options.text: In high gear the engine turns very slowly here, so its pushes are too weak and too far apart
High gear makes the engine spin too fast
options.feedback: It's the reverse: high gear lets the engine turn slowly for the wheels' speed. At walking pace, it's barely turning at all.

options.text: The steep slope stops the spark plugs from sparking
options.feedback: Sparks don't depend on the slope. Every cylinder still fires, just too rarely to keep the car climbing.

options.text: The gearbox has disconnected the engine from the wheels
options.feedback: If it had, the engine would turn freely without straining. The shudder shows it's struggling to turn the wheels.

challenge.hint: In high gear, how fast does the engine turn when the wheels turn slowly?
challenge.explanation: At walking pace, high gear leaves the engine turning so slowly that power strokes come too rarely to climb. A lower gear speeds the engine up.

takeaways: A petrol engine runs on thousands of tiny bursts of burning fuel and air, each pushing a piston down.
Each cylinder repeats four strokes (intake, compression, power, exhaust), and only the power stroke pushes.
The crankshaft turns the pushes into a spin; use low gears for strength and high gears for cruising.
